sourceEvidence.claim: BLOCK 1, ROW 2 — Beneficence: 'Do good.'; the special ethical (fiduciary) duty to act in the patient's best interest; the two collisions (autonomy — an informed patient has the right to decide; society — eg, mandatory TB treatment, traditionally patient interest supersedes) and the PRINCIPLE OF DOUBLE EFFECT — facilitating comfort is prioritized over potential side effects (eg, respiratory depression with opioid use) for patients receiving end-of-life care (em-dash as printed)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Beneficence

“Do good.” Physicians have a special ethical (fiduciary) duty to act in the patient’s best interest.
May conflict with autonomy (an informed patient has the right to decide) or what is best for
society (eg, mandatory TB treatment). Traditionally, patient interest supersedes.
Principle of double effect—facilitating comfort is prioritized over potential side effects (eg,
respiratory depression with opioid use) for patients receiving end-of-life care.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on the pinned page's lower portion (verify-evidence.ts)

kypExtensions.summary: The four-pillar grammar of the printed Core ethical principles table: AUTONOMY read through its three printed verbs (respect — truth-telling, confidentiality; create — informed consent; honor — accepting or NOT accepting care) as the HINGE principle, plus the collision resolution ladder — beneficence vs autonomy resolves 'an informed patient has the right to decide'; beneficence vs society (eg, mandatory TB treatment) resolves 'traditionally, patient interest supersedes'; risk vs benefit resolves through the informed patient proceeding ('most surgeries and medications fall into this category'); comfort vs side effects at end of life resolves through the principle of double effect; justice overlays distribution ('does not always imply equally (eg, triage)').
kypExtensions.rationale: The source prints the four definitions in parallel; the hinge reading, the three-verb decomposition of autonomy, the conflict-ladder organization, and the 'name the collision, apply the printed rule' protocol are KYP's synthesis.
kypExtensions.location: core.keyIdea MOVE 1 + mechanisms[0] principle-conflict-map + blocks[3] the decoder list block + the registry visual's Zone A pillars

kypExtensions.summary: The capacity-vs-competency see-saw: capacity = CLINICAL (a physician, at the bedside, for ONE specific healthcare-related decision, eg, to refuse medical care) vs competency = LEGAL (a judge, a GLOBAL ruling — legally unable to make any healthcare-related decision), plus the two guardrails read as wrong-answer killers — decisions made with capacity cannot be revoked simply if the patient later loses capacity (durability runs forward only), and diagnoses (intellectual disabilities, mental illnesses) are not exclusion criteria unless the condition presently impairs (test the patient, not the chart).
kypExtensions.rationale: The source prints the five paragraphs; the clinical-vs-legal framing, the decision-specificity emphasis, the 'guardrail' naming, and the forum/scope discriminator are KYP's organization.
kypExtensions.location: core.keyIdea MOVE 2 + mechanisms[1] capacity-assessment-flow + blocks[4] the compare block + the registry visual's Zone B see-saw and guardrail strip

kypExtensions.summary: The U-ARE bedside protocol: the printed four components (Understanding, Appreciation, Reasoning, Expressing a choice) sequenced as an ordered assessment — facts first, personalization second, comparison third, output last — with the rule that all four present → capacity for THIS decision and any one absent → impaired for that decision; the funnel framing (a patient can fail at any level while passing earlier ones) is KYP's.
kypExtensions.rationale: The source prints the four components and their questions as a side panel; the ordered protocol, the pass/fail rule, and the funnel framing are KYP's design.
kypExtensions.location: mechanisms[1] gate-components node + blocks[5] the steps block + the registry visual's Zone C strip + mnemonics[1] U-ARE

kypExtensions.summary: The pattern/trap/pivot/mini-case attack structure layered over the printed page — 4 patterns (the informed-refusal beneficence-vs-autonomy stem, the mandatory-TB beneficence-vs-society stem, the end-of-life opioid double-effect stem, the schizophrenia-refusal capacity-vs-competency stem), 4 traps (capacity vs competency; autonomy vs beneficence; diagnosis vs incapacity; nonmaleficence vs a risk veto), 3 pivots (chart-to-bedside on a psychiatric diagnosis; the yesterday-capable/today-confused irrevocability pivot; the judge/legally scope pivot), and 9 recall cards covering all three blocks.
kypExtensions.rationale: First Aid prints the principles and capacity rules only; the attack structure, distractor designs, and question shapes are KYP's design.

kypExtensions.summary: The mnemonic ledger: the page prints NO mnemonics of its own (VLM-confirmed — no red text, margin notes, or hooks in the lower portion; the mottos 'Do good.' and 'Do no harm.' are the Beneficence and Nonmaleficence openers, not mnemonics), so all FOUR codes are KYP originals, marked as such: 'A BRIGHT NEW JUDGE' (the four principles in printed order — Autonomy, Beneficence, Nonmaleficence, Justice), 'U-ARE' (Understanding, Appreciation, Reasoning, Expressing a choice), 'CAPACITY IS CLINICAL, COMPETENCY IS COURT' (physician/one decision vs judge/any decision), and 'COMFORT FIRST, PATIENT FIRST' (the double effect + the supersede rule).
